Weak Hopf non-invertible symmetry-protected topological spin liquid and lattice realization of (1+1)D symmetry topological field theory
Zhian Jia

Abstract
We propose weak Hopf symmetry as a general framework to explore (1+1)D topological phases that exhibit non-invertible symmetries. Inspired by the Symmetry Topological Field Theory (SymTFT) description of quantum phases with non-invertible symmetry, we construct a lattice model by introducing two distinct topological boundary conditions for a weak Hopf lattice gauge theory. One boundary encodes the topological symmetry information, while the other incorporates the non-topological dynamics. The resulting model is termed the cluster ladder model. We demonstrate that the cluster state model is a special case of this broader class of lattice models exhibiting weak Hopf symmetry H × H ^ H\times\hat{H} , where H H is a weak Hopf algebra and H ^ \hat{H} is its dual weak Hopf algebra. On a closed manifold, the symmetry reduces to Cocom ⁡ ( H ) × Cocom ⁡ ( H ^ ) \operatorname{Cocom}(H)\times\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H}) , corresponding to the cocommutative subalgebras of H × H ^ H\times\hat{H} . An essential weak Hopf sub-symmetry is Cocom ⁡ ( H ) × 𝖱𝖾𝗉 ⁡ ( H ) \operatorname{Cocom}(H)\times\mathsf{Rep}(H) , which, in the finite group case, reduces to the familiar symmetry G × 𝖱𝖾𝗉 ⁡ ( G ) G\times\mathsf{Rep}(G) . To exactly solve the lattice model, we introduce a weak Hopf tensor network. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to construct the lattice realization of an arbitrary fusion category symmetry 𝒮 \mathcal{S} via combining Tannaka–Krein reconstruction or weak Hopf tube algebra and the cluster ladder model.

Introduction

The symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases
[
1
,
2
,
3

have garnered significant attention in recent years. The ground state of an SPT phase is short-range entangled, and its topological order is characterized as an invertible topological order
[
12
,
13
]
. This implies that, on any closed manifold, SPT phases have a unique ground state.
Distinct SPT phases with a given symmetry cannot be smoothly deformed into each other without undergoing a phase transition, provided the deformation preserves the symmetry. However, if the symmetry is completely broken during the deformation, the SPT states can all be smoothly deformed into a product state.
The SPT phases are of particular interest due to their boundary behavior, the boundary of a SPT state is either gapless or degenerate.
The boundary effective theory of a non-trivial SPT state always exhibits a pure gauge anomaly or a mixed gauge-gravity anomaly with respect to the symmetry group
[
14
]
.
The classification of
d
-dimensional bosonic SPT phases with an internal symmetry group
G
is described by the group cohomology
H^{d+1}(G,U(1))

[
14
,
15
]
1
1

1

In this work,

denotes the spatial dimension, while

represents the spacetime dimension.

[

,
17
,

\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega_{d+1}^{G},U(1))

denotes the bordism group of
(d+1)
-dimensional manifolds with a

In Ref.

The concept of categorical symmetry can be understood through a holographic perspective

This approach, now referred to as symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT) or topological holography, provides a comprehensive framework for understanding non-invertible or categorical symmetries in both gapped and gapless phases

Consider an
n
-dimensional topological order,
the
(n-1)
-dimensional defects can be regarded as 1-morphisms,
(n-2)
-dimensional defects between
(n-1)
-dimensional defects can be regarded as 2-morphisms, and so on. Thus, the corresponding topological order is described by a fusion
n
-category
[
70
,
71
,
48
,
72
]
.
We can combine all
d
-dimensional topological orders to form a category
\mathbf{TO}_{d}
. For this category, we need to include domain walls between different topological orders and the stacking operation of topological orders to ensure that
\mathbf{TO}_{d}
is closed.
From Hamiltonian point of view, consider the moduli space
\mathfrak{M}_{nd}
formed by all
nd
gapped liquid Hamiltonians. An elements in
\pi_{0}(\mathfrak{M}_{nd})
is a topological order
[
73
,
74
,
75
]
.
Two topological orders are considered equivalent if they can be smoothly deformed into each other through a continuous path of Hamiltonians without closing the energy gap.
These equivalence classes of topological orders are described first fundamental group
\pi_{1}(\mathfrak{M})
. From algebraic point of view, two topological orders are equivalent if they can be connected by some invertible domain wall, the invertible domain walls are classified by
\pi_{1}(\mathfrak{M})
.
The
(n-1)
-dimensional defects can fuse but not braid. If we exclude these defects, we obtain a braided fusion
(n-1)
-category of excitations. This braided fusion category is the looping of the
n
-fusion category of topological order
[
48
,
72
]
.
A special type of topological order is called an invertible topological order
\mathcal{C}
, which is invertible under the stacking operation. Specifically, there exists a topological order
\mathcal{D}
such that the stacking of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
yields the trivial topological order:
\mathcal{C}\boxtimes\mathcal{D}\simeq\mathcal{I}
. The SPT phases possess exclusively invertible topological order, which guarantees the unique ground state of the SPT phase on any closed manifold.

For an
n
-dimensional system, its categorical symmetry is characterized by a fusion
n
-category
\mathcal{S}
. From a topological holography perspective, this fusion
n
-symmetry
\mathcal{S}
corresponds to an
(n+1)
-dimensional topological order, which is described by the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{S})
. Using the SymTFT sandwich construction
[

,

,

,
69
]
, this relationship can be understood as follows: the symmetry
\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{B}_{\text{sym}}
represents a topological boundary condition of the topological field theory
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{S})
. Additionally, there may exist another boundary,
\mathcal{B}_{\text{phys}}
, of
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{S})
, which encodes the non-topological aspects of the system. The boundary
\mathcal{B}_{\text{phys}}
can be either gapped or gapless.
For an
n=1
-dimensional system, the categorical symmetry is described by a fusion category
\mathcal{S}
(fusion 1-category). The symmetry is considered anomaly-free if there exists a 1-dimensional
\mathcal{S}
-SPT phase; otherwise, it is referred to as anomalous. For an anomaly-free
\mathcal{S}
, the
\mathcal{S}
-SPT phases are classified by fiber functors
F:\mathcal{S}\to\mathsf{Vect}
, which are tensor functors mapping
\mathcal{S}
to the category of finite-dimensional vector spaces
[
43
]
.

An interesting and challenging question is whether it is possible to construct a lattice model that realizes a given
\mathcal{S}
-SPT phase
[
76
,
77
,
46
,
78
,
79
,
80
,
59
,

,
88
,
89
]
. Despite the numerous examples of
\mathcal{S}
-symmetric phases, a systematic approach for constructing such models remains elusive. In this work, we address this question by exploring it within the framework of weak Hopf symmetry.

For a
(1+1)
D system, the categorical symmetry is described by a (multi)fusion category
\mathcal{S}
. It has been proven that any (multi)fusion category can be realized as the representation category of a weak Hopf algebra
[
90
,
91
,
92
]
. Motivated by this result, we introduce weak Hopf symmetries and use them to construct lattice models by generalizing the cluster state model.

The cluster state model is a widely studied example of lattice models exhibiting SPT phases. For the standard
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
cluster state, the Hamiltonian takes the form

H_{\mathrm{cluster}}=-\sum_{i}Z_{i-1}X_{i}Z_{i+1},

(1.1)

which is known to host
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
SPT order
[
93
]
.
By applying Hadamard gates to all even vertices of the lattice, one can map this system to the Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS)-type cluster state
[
94
,
80
,
56
]
. The stabilizers for the transformed state are of the CSS-type, specifically
X_{i-1}X_{i}X_{i+1}
for odd sites (
i\in 2\mathbb{N}+1
) and
Z_{i-1}Z_{i}Z_{i+1}
for even sites (
i\in 2\mathbb{N}
). This leads to a modified Hamiltonian of the form

H=-\sum_{i\in 2\mathbb{N}}Z_{i-1}Z_{i}Z_{i+1}-\sum_{i\in 2\mathbb{N}+1}X_{i-1}X_{i}X_{i+1}.

(1.2)

Recent studies have revealed that the cluster state model exhibits non-invertible global symmetries. In particular, the symmetry can be described by the fusion category
\mathsf{Rep}(D_{8})
, where
D_{8}
is the dihedral group of order 8
[
87
]
.

Since the qubit-based cluster state corresponds to systems valued in the Abelian group
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, a natural generalization is to consider systems defined over arbitrary finite groups
G

[
94
]
. This generalization involves introducing higher-dimensional analogs of Pauli operators, similar to those used in Kitaev’s quantum double model
[
95
,
96
]
.
The SPT order and non-invertible symmetries of such finite-group cluster states were recently analyzed in Ref.
[
80
]
. Using tensor network techniques, it was demonstrated that the symmetry of a
G
-valued cluster state is described by
G\times\mathsf{Rep}(G)
, where
\mathsf{Rep}(G)
is the representation category of
G
.
We generalize these results to the Hopf algebra setting in Ref.
[
56
]
.
Furthermore, Ref.
[
56
]
demonstrates that the cluster state model can be understood as a specific realization of a quantum double ladder model, which in turn provides a pathway for extending the construction to more general weak Hopf algebras (and even to weak quasi-Hopf algebras).

In this work, we systematically construct lattice models that realize an
\mathcal{S}
-symmetric phase (more precisely the phase with
\mathcal{S}
fusion algebra symmetry). To achieve this, we introduce a general framework for weak Hopf symmetric phases and demonstrate how such phases can be realized via SymTFT. We also show that the (multi)fusion symmetry can be interpreted as a dual weak Hopf symmetry.
Building on the observation that a cluster state SPT phase can be viewed as a thin quantum double model with one smooth and one rough boundary
[
56
]
, we introduce the
weak Hopf cluster state model
. Inspired by this construction, we further propose a generalized model, termed the
weak Hopf cluster ladder model
, where the two topological boundaries are chosen to be distinct and do not allow any non-trivial anyonic tunneling channels between them.
A crucial observation is that the symmetry of the (1+1)D cluster ladder model is given by
H\times\hat{H}
, where
H
represents a weak Hopf symmetry and
\hat{H}
is its dual weak Hopf symmetry. Notably, the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
symmetry of the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-cluster state, the
G\times\mathsf{Rep}(G)
symmetry of the
G
-cluster state model, and the
\operatorname{Cocom}(H)\times\mathsf{Rep}(H)
symmetry are all special cases of this general framework.
Also note that our model is quite different from that based on anyonic chains
[
81
,
82
,
83
,
59
,
64
]
, where the Hilbert space is constructed from the fusion tree and thus does not have a well-defined local space or tensor product structure
2
2

2

While a tensor product structure can be assigned to each edge, followed by a projection to enforce the two labels on the edge to be identical, this approach for introducing tensor product structure is not so natural.
.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section
2
, we use finite groups as examples to illustrate the key ideas of our lattice model. For the
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
group with
p
a prime number, there exists a single type of cluster ladder model, which corresponds to the
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
cluster state model. In contrast, for the
S_{3}
group, two distinct types of cluster ladder models that realize SPT phases arise: one corresponds to the cluster state model, while the other exhibits topological boundary conditions that differ from the conventional smooth and rough boundaries.
In Section
3
, we provide a detailed discussion of weak Hopf symmetries, introducing the necessary mathematical formalism and results. We begin with the case of invertible symmetries, which correspond to group algebra Hopf symmetries, and then extend the analysis to general weak Hopf symmetries and comodule algebra symmetries. Furthermore, we demonstrate how fusion category symmetries can be interpreted as dual weak Hopf symmetries. Finally, we explore the implications of weak Hopf symmetries for single-qudit systems.
Section
4
introduces weak Hopf tensor network states, which serve as a powerful tool for analyzing and solving our lattice model.
In Section
6
, we present the weak Hopf generalization of the cluster state model. The model is solved using weak Hopf tensor network states. We explore the weak Hopf symmetry of the model on both closed and open manifolds, demonstrating that there is a
H\times\hat{H}
symmetry for open manifolds, while for closed manifolds, the symmetry is given by
\operatorname{Cocom}(H)\times\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})
.
Section
7
extends the cluster state model to incorporate general boundary conditions. The lattice model is constructed using comodule algebras and can also be solved via weak Hopf tensor network states.
Finally, Section
9
provides a discussion of the results and outlines several open problems for future research.

2
Warm-up example: finite-group quantum cluster ladder

In Ref.
[
56
]
, it is demonstrated that the cluster state model is indeed a quantum double ladder model with rough and smooth boundaries. The aim of this paper is to generalize the construction presented therein to arbitrary weak Hopf algebras, encompassing all possible non-invertible symmetries in (1+1)D.
Before delving into the cluster ladder model realization of non-invertible symmetry for the most general weak Hopf case, let us first consider a warm-up example of the finite-group cluster ladder model, focusing specifically on the
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
and
S_{3}
quantum cluster ladder models. The finite-group cluster state model is also discussed in Refs.
[
94
,
80
]
. The macroscopic theory of the corresponding SymTFT is given in Ref.
[
58
]
. Here, we emphasize the comodule algebra approach and discuss it in a more general setting via the so-called quantum cluster ladder model.

The group-based Pauli X operators are defined as

\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|gh\rangle,\quad\overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|hg^{-1}\rangle.

(2.1)

For some irreducible representation
\Gamma\in\mathsf{Rep}(G)
, the group-based Pauli Z operators are defined by

Z_{\Gamma}=\sum_{g\in G}\Gamma(g)\otimes|g\rangle\langle g|,\quad Z^{\ddagger}_{\Gamma}=\sum_{g\in G}\Gamma(g^{-1})|g\rangle\langle g|.

(2.2)

If we take trace of the representation matrix, we obtain

\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\chi_{\Gamma}}=\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{\Gamma}(g)|g\rangle\langle g|,\quad\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\chi_{\Gamma}}=\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{\Gamma}(g^{-1})|g\rangle\langle g|,

(2.3)

where
\chi_{\Gamma}
is character of
\Gamma\in\mathsf{Rep}(G)
.

For a quantum double model
D(G)
of finite group
G
, the topological boundary conditions are determined by a pair
(K,\omega)
with
K
a subgroup of
G
and
\omega
a two-cocycle
[
95
,
97
,
98
,
99
]
.
The topological boundary conditions are equivalently classified by the comodule algebras over Hopf algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]

[
53
,
54
]
. Here for simplicity, we will only consider the case with trivial 2-cocycle.

(2.4)

For the symmetry boundary (blue edges), we place
K=\mathbb{C}[M]
on each edge. For the physical boundary (red edges), we place
J=\mathbb{C}[N]
on each edge. In the bulk (black edges), we assign
W=\mathbb{C}[G]
to each edge.
This means that the total Hilbert space is
\mathcal{H}_{\rm tot}=\text{H}_{\rm bk}\otimes\text{H}_{\rm sym}\otimes\text{H}_{\rm phys}
with
\text{H}_{\rm bk}=\otimes_{j}\mathbb{C}[G]
,
\text{H}_{\rm sym}=\otimes_{k}\mathbb{C}[M]
, and
\text{H}_{\rm phys}=\otimes_{l}\mathbb{C}[N]
.

The SymTFT bulk operator is the face operator which is defined as

\mathbb{B}_{f}=\sum_{\Gamma\in\operatorname{Irr}(G)}\frac{d_{\Gamma}}{|G|}\mathbb{B}_{f}^{\chi_{\Gamma}}

(2.7)

The physical boundary vertex operator is defined similarly. Both the face and vertex operators are equipped with a counterclockwise ordering (around the face and around the vertex). Alternatively, we can also define the model with a clockwise ordering.
The Hamiltonian is of the form

\mathbb{H}_{G}^{M,N}=\mathbb{H}_{\rm bk}+\mathbb{H}^{M}_{\rm sym}+\mathbb{H}^{N}_{\rm phys}

(2.8)

where
\mathbb{H}_{\rm bk}=\sum_{f}\mathbb{B}_{f}
,
\mathbb{H}_{\rm sym}=\sum_{v_{s}}\mathbb{A}_{v_{s}}
and
\mathbb{H}_{\rm phys}=\sum_{v_{p}}\mathbb{A}_{v_{p}}
. This model realize the SymTFT with fusion category symmetry give by the boundary excitations over the symmetry boundary.

The topological charges of the 2d bulk are labeled by the irreducible representations of the quantum double
D(G)

[
95
,
97
,
98
,
99
,
53
,
54
]
. These representations are classified by two components: the conjugacy class
[g]
of
G
, determining the magnetic charge, and the irreducible representations
\pi
of the centralizer
C_{G}([g])
, labeling the electric charge.
For symmetry boundaries
K=\mathbb{C}[M]
, the boundary excitation is described by the fusion category

\mathcal{B}_{\rm sym}={{}^{\mathbb{C}[G]}_{K}}\mathsf{Mod}_{K},

(2.9)

which is the category of
\mathbb{C}[G]
-covariant
K|K
-bimodules
[
100
,
53
,
54
]
. The boundary excitations are equivalently classified by pairs
(S,\pi)
, where
S\in M\backslash G/M
is a double coset and
\pi
is an irreducible representation of
M\cap rMr^{-1}
, with
r\in S

[
98
]
. For physical boundaries
J=\mathbb{C}[N]
, the excitations can be characterized in a similar manner.
Since we have chosen both boundaries to be topological boundaries, the cluster ladder model exhibits the following symmetry
3
3

3

This reflects the fact that, in a lattice model, one cannot distinguish which topological boundary is a symmetry boundary, as both boundaries are on equal footing.
:

\mathcal{B}_{\rm sym}\times\mathcal{B}_{\rm phys}={{}^{\mathbb{C}[G]}_{K}}\mathsf{Mod}_{K}\times{{}_{J}}\mathsf{Mod}^{\mathbb{C}[G]}_{J},

(2.10)

where
\mathbb{C}[G]
is placed on the left and right, respectively, to emphasize that
K
is a left
\mathbb{C}[G]
-comodule algebra and
J
is a right
\mathbb{C}[G]
-comodule algebra.

The CSS-type cluster state model is a special case of the quantum cluster ladder model, featuring one rough boundary and one smooth boundary
[
56
]
.
For this case,
M=G
and
N=\{1\}
. The symmetry boundary excitation becomes
\mathcal{B}_{\rm sym}=\mathsf{Rep}(G)
, while the physical boundary excitation becomes
\mathsf{Vect}_{G}
, the category of
G
-graded vector spaces.
Notice that for the rough boundary edge, the boundary space reduces to
\mathbb{C}
, allowing us to effectively remove it. Additionally,
\mathbb{A}_{v_{p}}
becomes the identity operator, so we can also remove the boundary vertex operator. The lattice then simplifies to:

(2.11)

and the corresponding Hamiltonian becomes

\mathbb{H}_{G}^{G,\{1\}}=-\sum_{f}\mathbb{B}_{f}^{G}-\sum_{v_{s}:\text{sym}}\mathbb{A}^{G}_{v_{s}}.

(2.12)

The symmetry of the model is

\mathcal{B}_{\rm sym}\times\mathcal{B}_{\rm phys}=\mathsf{Rep}(G)\times\mathsf{Vect}_{G}.

(2.13)

Notice that choosing different configurations of orientations for each edge results in distinct cluster state models, and choosing a clockwise local ordering also yields a different model. However, all these models realize the same phase. The models discussed in Refs.
[
80
,
56
]
are examples of the clockwise model. In this paper, we follow the conventions in Refs.
[
95
,
53
,
54
]
by using the counterclockwise local ordering. This will be elaborated in more detail later when discussing weak Hopf cluster ladder models.

2.1
Abelian cluster ladder model

Consider the
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
quantum double model, where
p
is a prime number.
4
4

4

We consider this case since there are only two possible topological boundary conditions; the discussion can be generalized to a general Abelian group straightforwardly.

The topological charges are given by irreducible representations of
D(\mathbb{Z}_{p})
:

a_{[g],\pi_{h}}=e^{g}\otimes m^{h}=:\varepsilon^{g,h},g,h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

(2.14)

Since
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
is Abelian,
[g]
consists of a single element
\{g\}
and
C_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}([g])=\mathbb{Z}_{p}
. The irreducible representations of the Abelian group are also labeled by elements
h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}
.
The fusion rule reads

\varepsilon^{g,h}\otimes\varepsilon^{k,l}=(e^{g}\otimes m^{h})\otimes(e^{k}\otimes m^{l})=e^{g+k}\otimes m^{h+l}=\varepsilon^{g+k,h+l},

(2.15)

namely, they form
\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p}
fusion algebra. In a good choice of gauge, the fusion F-symbols are trivial (i.e., they equal to 1 when allowed by fusion), and the braiding R-symbols read

R_{\varepsilon^{g,h},\varepsilon^{k,l}}=\exp(\frac{2\pi i}{p}gl).

(2.16)

There are two possible topological boundary conditions of the
D(\mathbb{Z}_{p})
quantum double model:

•

Rough boundary
(
Dirichlet boundary
): This corresponds to the trivial subgroup
M_{r}=\{0\}
5
5

5

Here we use
0
to denote the identity of the group.
.
The Lagrangian algebra is
\mathcal{A}_{r}=\mathbb{1}\oplus e\oplus\cdots\oplus e^{p-1}
meaning all electric charges condense on this boundary. The boundary excitation is given by the unitary fusion category
\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}]^{\vee})
, where
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}]^{\vee}
denotes the dual algebra of
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}]
.

•

Smooth boundary
(
Neumann boundary
): This corresponds to the subgroup
N_{s}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}
. The Lagrangian algebra is
\mathcal{A}_{s}=\mathbb{1}\oplus m\oplus\cdots\oplus m^{p-1}
, meaning all magnetic fluxes condense on this boundary. The boundary excitation is given by
\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}])
.

In both cases, the associated 2-cocycles are trivial. The triviality of the 2-cocycle can be understood as follows:
the case of
H^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{1},\mathbb{C}^{\times})=0
is straightforwardly trivial. For
H^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{p},\mathbb{C}^{\times})
, we use the relation

H^{n}(G,\mathbb{Z})\simeq H^{n-1}(G,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\simeq H^{n-1}(G,\mathbb{C}^{\times}),\quad\text{for all }n\geq 2,

along with the fact that
H^{3}(\mathbb{Z}_{p},\mathbb{Z})=0
.

For the Abelian group
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
, the Weyl-Heisenberg
X
operator is given by

X_{g}=\sum_{h\in G}|h+g\rangle\langle h|,

where
X_{g}=\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{g}
and
X_{g}^{\dagger}=\overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}
. Recall that all irreducible representations (irreps) of
\mathbb{Z}_{p}
are one-dimensional, and
\chi_{\Gamma}
is a complex character function, with
\Gamma_{k}
labeled by a group element
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}
. In this way,
\chi_{k}(h)=\exp(2\pi ikh/p)
.
The Weyl-Heisenberg
Z
operator is defined as

Z_{k}=\sum_{h\in G}\chi_{k}(h)|h\rangle\langle h|,

where
Z_{k}=\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma_{k}}
and
Z_{k}^{\dagger}=\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma_{k}}
.

The face operator in this case can be simplified as
\mathbb{B}_{f}^{\chi_{\Gamma}}=\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{k}\otimes\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{k}\otimes\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{k}
:

(2.17)

Thus, the face operator is given by

\mathbb{B}_{f}=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{k}\otimes\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{k}\otimes\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{k}.

The symmetry boundary operator becomes

\mathbb{A}_{v_{s}}=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{g\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}\otimes\overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}\otimes\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{g}.

This model is nothing but the cluster state model
[
56
,
80
,
94
]
.
The symmetry of the model is
\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})\times\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}
, with the fusion algebra
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}))=\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}})=\mathbb{Z}_{p}
(we use
\operatorname{Gr}
to denote Grothendieck group), which gives the usual
\mathbb{Z}_{p}\times\mathbb{Z}_{p}
cluster state model.

2.2
S_{3}
cluster ladder model

For non-Abelian group
S_{3}=\langle\sigma,\tau:\sigma^{2}=\tau^{3}=1,\sigma\tau=\tau^{-1}\sigma\rangle
(we take
\sigma=(12)
and
\tau=(123)
), the corresponding quantum double model
D(S_{3})
has eight topological charges described in the following table:

\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{|c|ccc|cc|ccc|}\hline\cr&A&B&C&D&E&F&G&H\\
\hline\cr\text{conjugacy class}~[g]&[1]&[1]&[1]&[\sigma]&[\sigma]&[\tau]&[\tau]&[\tau]\\
\text{irrep of the centralizer}&\mathbb{1}&\mathrm{sign}&\pi&\omega_{2}^{0}&\omega_{2}^{1}&\omega_{3}^{0}&\omega_{3}^{1}&\omega_{3}^{2}\\
\hline\cr\end{array}

Notice
C_{S_{3}}([1])=S_{3}
, we use
\mathbb{1}
to denote the trivial irrep,
\mathrm{sign}
to denote the sign representation, and
\pi
to denote the two-dimensional representation of
S_{3}
.
For
C_{S_{3}}([\sigma])=\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, we use
\omega_{2}^{0}
and
\omega_{2}^{1}
to denote the two irreducible representations (irreps) of
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
(
\omega_{2}
is the second root of unity).
For
C_{S_{3}}([\tau])=\mathbb{Z}_{3}
, we use
\omega_{3}^{k}
, where
k=0,1,2
, to denote its three irreps (
\omega_{3}
is the third root of unity). Their fusion rules are given in Table

The

and

S=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2&3&3&2&2&2\\

(2.18)

Notice that the first row of the
S
-matrix represents the quantum dimensions of all topological charges, while the
T
-matrix encodes the topological spins of these charges. The fusion rule
N_{XY}^{Z}
can be determined from the
S
-matrix using the Verlinde formula:

\displaystyle N_{XY}^{Z}=\sum_{U\in\operatorname{Irr}(D(G))}\frac{S_{XU}S_{YU}S_{ZU}^{\ast}}{S_{\mathbb{1}U}},

(2.20)

where the summation runs over all irreducible representations
U
, and
\mathbb{1}
denotes the trivial charge.
For more details of modular data, see Refs.
[
102
,
103
,
104
]
.

There are four types of topological boundary conditions
[
98
]
:

•

Rough boundary
: This corresponds to the trivial subgroup
M_{r}=\{1\}
. The Lagrangian algebra is
\mathcal{A}_{r}=A\oplus B\oplus 2C
. The boundary excitation is given by
\mathsf{Vect}_{S_{3}}
.

•

Smooth boundary
: This corresponds to the trivial subgroup
M_{s}=S_{3}
. The Lagrangian algebra is
\text{A}_{s}=A\oplus D\oplus F
. The boundary excitation is given by
\mathsf{Rep}(S_{3})
.

•

\mathbb{Z}_{2}
boundary
: This corresponds to the subgroup
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
of
S_{3}
. The Lagrangian algebra is
\text{A}_{2}=A\oplus C\oplus D
.

•

\mathbb{Z}_{3}
boundary
: This corresponds to the subgroup
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
of
S_{3}
. The Lagrangian algebra is
\text{A}_{3}=A\oplus B\oplus 2F
.

For the cluster ladder lattice, if there is no anyonic tunneling channel between the two boundaries, the ground state degeneracy of the model is 1. Such a model is a candidate for a non-invertible SPT phase. This includes the following models:

1.

The smooth and rough boundary pair:

\mathbb{H}[\text{A}_{s},\text{A}_{r}]
. This corresponds to the
S_{3}
cluster state model. The symmetry is given by
\mathsf{Rep}(S_{3})\times\mathsf{Vect}_{S_{3}}
.

2.

The
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
and
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
boundary pair:

\mathbb{H}[\text{A}_{2},\text{A}_{3}]
. This model is entirely different from the cluster state model. Its symmetry is given by
\mathsf{Rep}(D(S_{3}))_{\text{A}_{2}}\times\mathsf{Rep}(D(S_{3}))_{\text{A}_{3}}
, where we use the notation
\mathsf{Rep}(D(S_{3}))_{\text{A}}
to denote the category of
𝒜
-modules in
\mathsf{Rep}(D(S_{3}))
. Equivalently, the symmetry can be described as
{{}^{\mathbb{C}[S_{3}]}_{K}}\mathsf{Mod}_{K}\times{{}_{J}}\mathsf{Mod}^{\mathbb{C}[S_{3}]}_{J}
, where
K=\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{2}]
and
J=\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{3}]
.

The lattice model with
\mathsf{Rep}(S_{3})
symmetry has been discussed carefully based on the anyonic chain in Ref.
[
59
]
. Our model here can be regarded as an alternative lattice realization.

For other pairings, we also provide the corresponding lattice Hamiltonian, e.g.,
\mathbb{H}[\text{A}_{r},\text{A}_{2}]
,
\mathbb{H}[\text{A}_{s},\text{A}_{3}]
, etc. Due to the existence of anyonic tunneling channels between the two boundaries, the symmetry is either fully or partially broken.

3
Weak Hopf non-invertible symmetry

From a modern perspective, symmetries can be characterized by the algebraic structure of topological defects
[
27
,
57
,
48
,
36
,
58
,
59
,
60
,
61
,
62
,
63
,
64
,
65
,
66
,
67
,
42
,
41
]
.
Symmetries associated with non-invertible topological defects are known as non-invertible symmetries. For (1+1)D system, the symmetry is described by a fusion
1
-category, viz., the usual fusion category, thus it’s also called fusion category symmetry
[
41
,
42
,
43
]
.
Since any unitary (multi)fusion category is equivalent to the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
for some weak Hopf algebra
H
, it is natural for us to investigate the symmetry in the framework of Hopf and weak Hopf algebras
[
95
,
49
,
105
,
50
,
106
,
53
,
54
,
55
,
56
]
. These symmetries, characterized by quantum algebras such as Hopf, quasi-Hopf and weak Hopf algebras, as well as module and comodule algebras over (weak, quasi-) Hopf algebras, constitute a significant class of non-invertible symmetries
[
31
,
32
,
33
,
34
,
35
,
36
,
30
]
.

As we will see, in many cases, by fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(H)
, people usually refer to the fusion algebra symmetry, whose algebraic structure is the fusion ring (Grothendieck ring)
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
of the category
\mathcal{C}
(or more generally,
R(\mathcal{C})=\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}
). This fusion ring can be naturally embedded into the dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
. This suggests that weak Hopf symmetry provides a comprehensive framework for understanding non-invertible fusion algebra symmetries in (1+1)D systems.

3.1
Weak Hopf algebra symmetry and weak Hopf comodule algebra symmetry

Here, we will review the definitions of various quantum algebras used in this work and discuss the symmetries characterized by these algebras. For further details on quantum algebras, see, e.g., Refs.
[
107
,
108
,
109
,
110
]
.
Notice that, unless otherwise specified, all algebras and categories in this work are over the complex number field
\mathbb{C}
.

3.1.1
Hopf symmetry

A complex Hopf algebra is a complex vector space
H
equipped with the five structure linear morphisms: multiplication
\mu:H\otimes H\to H
, unit
\eta:\mathbb{C}\to H
, comultiplication
\Delta:H\to H\otimes H
, counit
\varepsilon:H\to\mathbb{C}
, and antipode
S:H\to H
. These maps satisfy the following conditions:

1.

(H,\mu,\eta)
is an algebra, meaning
\mu\circ(\mu\otimes\operatorname{id})=\mu\circ(\operatorname{id}\otimes\mu)
and
\mu\circ(\eta\otimes\operatorname{id})=\operatorname{id}=\mu\circ(\operatorname{id}\otimes\eta)
.

2.

(H,\Delta,\varepsilon)
is a coalgebra, meaning
(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta
and
(\varepsilon\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta=\operatorname{id}=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta
.

3.

(H,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon)
forms a bialgebra, where
\Delta
and
\varepsilon
are algebra homomorphisms, and equivalently,
\mu
and
\eta
are coalgebra homomorphisms.

4.

The antipode
S
satisfies
\mu\circ(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=\mu\circ(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\circ\Delta
.

We will use the notation
\mu(x\otimes y)=xy
and
\eta(1)=1_{H}
for multiplication and unit. We will also adopt the Sweedler’s notation
\Delta(u)=\sum_{(u)}u^{(1)}\otimes u^{(2)}=\sum_{i}u_{i}^{(1)}\otimes u_{i}^{(2)}
. The comultiplication law ensures that
(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta(u)=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta(u)=\sum_{(u)}u^{(1)}\otimes u^{(2)}\otimes u^{(3)}
.
In general, we define
\Delta_{1}=\Delta
and
\Delta_{n}=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\cdots\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta_{n-1}
, then
\Delta_{n}(u)=\sum_{(u)}u^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u^{(n+1)}
. From the definition above, we have the following useful identity:

\displaystyle\sum_{(x)}\varepsilon(x^{(1)})x^{(2)}=x=\sum_{(x)}x^{(1)}\varepsilon(x^{(2)}).

(3.1)

The swap operation is defined as
\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x
, by which one denotes
\mu^{\rm op}=\mu\circ\tau
and
\Delta^{\rm op}=\tau\circ\Delta
. The opposite Hopf algebra
H^{\rm op}
is defined as
(H,\mu^{\rm op},\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon,S^{-1})
, and the coopposite weak Hopf algebra
H^{\rm cop}
is defined as
(H,\mu,\eta,\Delta^{\rm op},\varepsilon,S^{-1})
. For more details about our notation and convention, see
[
53
,
54
,
56
]
.

Definition 1

(Hopf symmetry)
.

A quantum system
(\mathbb{H},\mathcal{H})
is said to exhibit Hopf symmetry if and only if the Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
supports a representation of a Hopf algebra, given by
W_{\bullet}:H\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{H})
, and satisfies the following conditions:
(i)
[W_{h},\mathbb{H}]=0
for all
h\in H
;
(ii) all eigenspaces
\mathcal{V}
of
\mathbb{H}
are invariant under the
H
-action.
This symmetry will also be referred to as Hamiltonian symmetry to distinguish it from state symmetry.

In certain cases (especially when discussing weak Hopf symmetry), it is useful to discuss symmetry within the vacuum space. Specifically, this refers to an operator
W_{h}
that commutes with the Hamiltonian
\mathbb{H}
only within the ground state space, i.e.,

[W_{h},\mathbb{H}]_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{GS}}}=0,\quad\forall h\in H.

The ground state symmetry is generally larger than the Hamiltonian symmetry defined above.

All group symmetries are special cases of Hopf symmetries. A key example of a non-group Hopf algebra symmetry is quantum double symmetry
D(G)
.
Consider a
(2+1)
D discrete gauge theory, such as Gauge-Higgs theory, where a Higgs field breaks the continuous gauge group
U
to a finite group
G

[
111
,
112
]
. In the low-energy or long-distance limit, the theory becomes topological, with excitations characterized by fusion and braiding data. These data are captured by the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(D(G))
, corresponding to the quantum double of
G
.
This formalism is generalized in
[
49
]
, where the unbroken symmetry is described by a Hopf algebra
H
, of which the group algebra is a special case.
Hopf algebraic symmetry has broad applications in quantum gravity
[
113
,
107
,
114
]
, conformal field theory (CFT)
[
115
]
, topological quantum field theory (TQFT)
[
116
,
105
]
, and the quantum Hall effect
[
117
]
.
The Hopf quantum double model provides a general framework for realizing Hopf symmetry
[
95
,
50
,
118
,
105
,
116
,
119
,
106
,
120
,
51
,
53
]
, while certain string-net models exhibit Hopf symmetry
[
121
,
55
]
, among other examples.

Invertible Hopf symmetry

A special type of Hopf symmetry is the conventional invertible group symmetry, where
H=\mathbb{C}[G]
. The group elements form a basis, with multiplication induced by group multiplication. The comultiplication and counit are defined as
\Delta(g)=g\otimes g
and
\varepsilon(g)=1
for all basis elements
g\in G
. The antipode is given by
S(g)=g^{-1}
for each
g\in G
, and the
*
-operation (to be defined later for more general weak Hopf algebras) is specified by
g^{*}=g^{-1}
.

Recall that for invertible symmetry
G
,
U_{g}^{\dagger}=U_{g^{*}}=U_{g^{-1}}
.
U_{g}
’s commute with Hamiltonian
\mathbb{H}
for all
g\in G
. The total Hilbert space supports a representation of
G
, and all eigenspace of
\mathbb{H}
is invariant under the
G
-action. When regarded as a group algebra symmetry
\mathbb{C}[G]
, we say
(\mathbb{H},\mathcal{H})
possesses a
\mathbb{C}[G]
symmetry means that (i)
[U_{x},\mathbb{H}]=0
for all
x\in\mathbb{C}[G]
; (ii) any eigenspace
\mathcal{V}
of
\mathbb{H}
is invariant under the
G
-action, note that this a result of condition (i).

A natural question now arises: under what circumstances is a Hopf symmetry invertible? We provide the following formal definition:

Definition 2
.

A (weak) Hopf symmetry
H
is called
invertible
if there exists a group
G
such that
H\cong\mathbb{C}[G]
as Hopf algebras.

Notice that the elements in
G
are all invertible, but the elements in
\mathbb{C}[G]
are generally not invertible.
Determining whether a given Hopf symmetry is invertible is generally a challenging task. It is clear that group algebra symmetries must be cocommutative.
For pointed cocommutative Hopf symmetries
6
6

6

A Hopf algebra
H
over a field
\mathbb{F}
is called pointed if all its simple left or right comodules are one-dimensional. See Ref.
[
122
]
for more details.
, a useful result is the Cartier-Konstant-Milnor-Moore theorem
[
123
,
124
,
125
,
104
]
.

For a (weak) Hopf algebra
H
, an element
g\in H
is called a group-like element if and only if
\Delta(g)=g\otimes g
and
\varepsilon(g)=1
. The set of all group-like elements of
H
is denoted by
\mathcal{G}(H)
; it forms a group when the antipode
S
is invertible. If
x\in H
satisfies
\Delta(x)=x\otimes 1+1\otimes x
, we call
x
a primitive element. If
x
is primitive, then we have
\varepsilon(x)=0
. The set of all primitive element of
H
is denoted as
\mathcal{P}(H)
, and
\mathcal{P}(H)
is a Lie algebra with
[x,y]:=xy-yx
. For group algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]
, it is clear that
\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{C}[G])=\{0\}
and
\mathcal{G}(\mathbb{C}[G])=G
.

The Cartier-Konstant-Milnor-Moore theorem
[
123
,
124
,
125
,
104
]
claims that, for pointed cocommutative Hopf algebras
H
, we have

H\cong U(\mathcal{P}(H))\#\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{G}(H)],

(3.2)

where
\mathcal{P}(H)
is the set of primitive elements of
H
,
U(\mathcal{P}(H))
is the universal enveloping algebra of
\mathcal{P}(H)
, and
\mathcal{G}(H)
is the set of group elements in
H
; ‘#’ represents smash product (see, e.g.,
[
109
]
).

Since
\mathcal{P}(H)=0
for a finite-dimensional complex Hopf algebra
H

[
126
, Exercise 4.2.16]
, a direct consequence of the Cartier–Kostant–Milnor–Moore theorem is that for finite-dimensional pointed cocommutative Hopf algebras, we have
H\cong\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{G}(H)]
. Therefore, all finite-dimensional pointed cocommutative Hopf symmetries are invertible symmetries.

Comodule algebra symmetry

As shown in Refs.
[
53
,
54
,
55
]
, (weak) Hopf symmetry characterizes 2d topologically ordered phases, while 1d gapped boundaries exhibit comodule algebra symmetry (or equivalently, module algebra symmetry). These symmetries are fundamental to our construction of non-invertible SPT lattice models. We now review their definitions.

Let
H
be a Hopf algebra, and let
(K,\mu_{K},\eta_{K})
be an algebra. If
K
is a left
H
-comodule with coaction
\beta_{K}:K\to H\otimes K

7
7

7

This means that
(\operatorname{id}\otimes\beta)\circ\beta=(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\beta
and
(\varepsilon\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\beta=\operatorname{id}
.
, satisfying the conditions:

\beta_{K}(xy)=\beta_{K}(x)\beta_{K}(y),\quad\beta_{K}(1_{K})=1_{H}\otimes 1_{K},

(3.3)

then
K
is called a
left
H
-comodule algebra
. A
right
H
-comodule algebra
can be defined analogously.
For left and right comodules, we adopt Sweedler’s notation for left and right coactions as follows:

\displaystyle\beta(x)=\sum_{(x)}x^{[-1]}\otimes x^{[0]},\beta(x)=\sum_{(x)}x^{[0]}\otimes x^{[1]}.

(3.4)

Let
H
be a Hopf algebra and
M
an algebra. If
M
is a left
H
-module and satisfies the following conditions:

h\triangleright(xy)=\sum_{(h)}(h^{(1)}\triangleright x)(h^{(2)}\triangleright y),\quad h\triangleright 1_{M}=\varepsilon(h)1_{M},

(3.5)

for all
h\in H
and
x,y\in M
, then
M
is called a
left
H
-module algebra
. A
right
H
-module algebra
is defined similarly.

From a macroscopic perspective, the description of the 1d gapped boundary of the quantum double model in terms of comodule algebra and module algebra is equivalent. Henceforth, following the convention in Refs.
[
53
,
54
,
55
]
, we adopt the comodule algebra description.

3.1.2
Weak Hopf symmetries

It is well-known that not all fusion categories can be regarded as the representation category of a Hopf algebra. Typical examples include the Haagerup category and
\mathsf{Vect}_{G}^{\omega}
(the category of
G
-graded vector spaces with a non-trivial 3-cocycle
\omega
). To represent an arbitrary fusion category as a representation category, it is necessary to introduce the concept of weak Hopf algebras
[
90
,
91
,
92
]
.

A complex weak Hopf algebra
[
127
]
is a complex vector space equipped with the same structural morphisms as a Hopf algebra, but with modified compatibility conditions:

1.

The triple
(H,\mu,\eta)
is an algebra, and the triple
(H,\Delta,\varepsilon)
forms a coalgebra.

2.

The quintuple
(H,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\varepsilon)
is a weak bialgebra, meaning that the algebra structure and coalgebra structure are compatible in the following way:

(i)
Multiplicativity of comultiplication:
The comultiplication map satisfies
\Delta(xy)=\Delta(x)\cdot\Delta(y)
, explicitly,

\sum_{(x\cdot y)}(x\cdot y)^{(1)}\otimes(x\cdot y)^{(2)}=\sum_{(x),(y)}x^{(1)}\cdot y^{(1)}\otimes x^{(2)}\cdot y^{(2)}.

(3.6)

This property holds for Hopf algebras as well.

(ii)
Weak comultiplicativity of the unit:
The comultiplication of the identity element satisfies

(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\Delta(1_{H})=(\Delta(1_{H})\otimes 1_{H})\cdot(1_{H}\otimes\Delta(1_{H}))=(1_{H}\otimes\Delta(1_{H}))\cdot(\Delta(1_{H})\otimes 1_{H}).

(3.7)

This indicates that the comultiplication of the identity is not factorizable but instead takes the form of a linear combination:

\Delta(1_{H})=\sum_{(1_{H})}1_{H}^{(1)}\otimes 1_{H}^{(2)}.

(3.8)

In the case of Hopf algebras, we have the stronger condition

\Delta(1_{H})=1_{H}\otimes 1_{H}.

(3.9)

(iii)
Weak multiplicativity of the counit:
For all
x,y,z\in H
, the counit satisfies

\varepsilon(x\cdot y\cdot z)=\sum_{(y)}\varepsilon(x\cdot y^{(1)})\varepsilon(y^{(2)}\cdot z)=\sum_{(y)}\varepsilon(x\cdot y^{(2)})\varepsilon(y^{(1)}\cdot z).

(3.10)

For Hopf algebras, since
\Delta(1_{H})=1_{H}\otimes 1_{H}
, setting
y=1
in the above equation gives the stronger constraint
\varepsilon(xz)=\varepsilon(x)\varepsilon(z)
.

3.

The antipode
S
plays the role of taking the inverse of elements, and its axioms differ significantly from those of Hopf algebras. It satisfies the following properties:

(i)
Left counit:
For all
x
in
H
, we have

\sum_{(x)}x^{(1)}S(x^{(2)})=\varepsilon_{L}(x):=\sum_{(1_{H})}\varepsilon(1_{H}^{(1)}x)1_{H}^{(2)}.

(3.11)

For Hopf algebras, we have the stronger relation
\sum_{(x)}x^{(1)}S(x^{(2)})=\varepsilon_{L}(x)=\varepsilon(x)1_{H}
.

(ii)
Right counit:
For all
x
in
H
, we have

\sum_{(x)}S(x^{(1)})x^{(2)}=\varepsilon_{R}(x):=\sum_{(1_{H})}1_{H}^{(1)}\varepsilon(x1_{H}^{(2)}).

(3.12)

For Hopf algebra, we have the stronger relation
\sum_{(x)}S(x^{(1)})x^{(2)}=\varepsilon_{R}(x)=\varepsilon(x)1_{H}
.

(iii)
Antipode decomposition:
For all
x
in
H
, we have

\sum_{(x)}S(x^{(1)})x^{(2)}S(x^{(3)})=S(x).

(3.13)

This condition also holds for Hopf algebras.

Notice that the images of the left and right counit maps are denoted as
H_{L}=\varepsilon_{L}(H)
and
H_{R}=\varepsilon_{R}(H)
. They serve as the tensor unit (vacuum charge or vacuum sector) of the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
of
H
. In general, the tensor unit is not simple, and the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
is a multifusion category. When
H
is connected
[
92
]
(also called pure in Ref.
[
127
]
),
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
is a fusion category.
If the dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
is connected, we call
H
coconnected
[
128
]
. In this work, we primarily consider connected and coconnected weak Hopf algebras, although all discussions can be straightforwardly generalized.

We will also assume that the weak Hopf algebra is a
C^{*}
-weak Hopf algebra. A complex weak Hopf algebra
H
is called simple (or indecomposable) if its underlying algebra
(H,\mu,\eta)
has no nontrivial subalgebras, and it is called semisimple if its underlying algebra can be written as a direct sum of simple algebras.
A
*
-weak Hopf algebra
(H,*)
is a weak Hopf algebra
H
equipped with a
C^{*}
-structure
*:H\to H
such that
\Delta
is a
*
-homomorphism. That is, for all
x,y\in H
and
c\in\mathbb{C}
,

(x^{*})^{*}=x,\quad(x+y)^{*}=x^{*}+y^{*},\quad(xy)^{*}=y^{*}x^{*},\quad(cx)^{*}=\bar{c}x^{*},\quad\Delta(x)^{*}=\Delta(x^{*}).

(3.14)

We also have

S(x^{*})=S^{-1}(x)^{*}.

(3.15)

A
C^{*}
-weak Hopf algebra
(H,*)
is one for which there exists a fully faithful
*
-representation
\rho:H\to\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{H})
for some operator space over a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
.

The weak Hopf morphism between two weak Hopf algebras
H_{1}
and
H_{2}
is a map
f:H_{1}\to H_{2}
which is both an algebra and coalgebra homomorphism preserving unit and counit and which intertwines the antipodes,
f\circ S_{1}=S_{2}\circ f
. The category of all finite dimensional weak Hopf algebras will be denoted as
\mathsf{WeakHopfAlg}_{\mathbb{C}}
.

A weak Kac algebra is a weak Hopf algebra such that
S^{2}=\operatorname{id}

[
129
,
130
]
. All finite-dimensional semisimple Hopf algebras are weak Kac algebras due to the Larson-Radford theorem (See, e.g., Ref.
[
110
]
).

Definition 3

(Weak Hopf symmetry)
.

A Hamiltonian
\mathbb{H}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}
is said to possess weak Hopf symmetry
H
if
\mathcal{H}
supports a representation
W_{\bullet}:H\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal{H})
of the weak Hopf algebra
H
, such that
[W_{h},\mathbb{H}]=0
for all
h\in H
.
In some contexts, we consider symmetries that act only on the ground states, where
[\mathbb{H},W_{h}]=0
holds (at least) within the ground state space
\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}
.
In such cases, the symmetry of the ground state space must be larger than that of the Hamiltonian, i.e.,
\operatorname{Sym}_{\rm GS}\supseteq\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathbb{H}}
.
If the ground state space is non-degenerate, meaning
\dim\mathcal{V}_{\rm GS}=1
, the ground state must be an eigenstate of the symmetry operator
W_{h}
.
When the weak Hopf algebra is a weak Kac algebra, we refer to the corresponding symmetry as weak Kac symmetry.

To summarize, the hierarchy of symmetries is as follows:

\text{Invertible symmetry}\subset\text{Hopf symmetry}\subset\text{Weak Kac symmetry}\subset\text{Weak Hopf symmetry}.

(3.16)

For weak Hopf symmetry, the notion of invariance under the symmetry action differs from that of groups and Hopf algebras
[
54
]
. A state
|\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}
is called left-invariant under the action if and only if

W_{h}|\psi\rangle=W_{\varepsilon_{L}(h)}|\psi\rangle.

(3.17)

The notion of right-invariance is defined analogously.
For a Hopf algebra, Eq. (
3.17
) reduces to

W_{h}|\psi\rangle=\varepsilon(h)|\psi\rangle,\quad\forall h\in H,

(3.18)

which means that
|\psi\rangle
is an eigenstate of
W_{h}
with eigenvalue
\varepsilon(h)
.
For a group algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]
, where
\varepsilon(g)=1
for all
g\in G
, this further simplifies to the usual definition of invariance for group symmetries.

Notice that the above definition applies to a quantum mechanical system, which can be viewed as a
(0+1)
D quantum field theory. In this case, issues of locality do not arise. However, when considering lattice models in higher dimensions, locality becomes a crucial ingredient. A promising approach to encode locality in both quantum field theory and lattice models is via quasi-local algebras (a type of AF-algebra). Yet, for non-invertible symmetries—which are intrinsically non-local, in the sense that they act over long distances—the quasi-local algebra framework appears insufficient. This suggests that a new mathematical structure may be required in order to incorporate non-invertible symmetries and locality within the AQFT framework. The locality structure is also crucial for discussing anomalies of symmetry.
We will return to the locality structure in the context of our model later on.

Weak Hopf comodule algebra symmetry

For the topological boundary condition of
2d
weak Hopf lattice gauge theory, we require the concept of a comodule algebra over weak Hopf algebras
[
54
]
. The axioms for the comodule algebra need to be adjusted compared to the standard Hopf algebra case.

Definition 4
.

Let
H
be a weak Hopf algebra, an algebra
K
is called a left
H
-comodule algebra
[
131
]
if there exists a comodule map
\beta:K\to H\otimes K
such that

\beta(xy)=\beta(x)\beta(y),

(3.19)

and

(1_{H}\otimes x)\beta(1_{K})=(\varepsilon_{R}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})\circ\beta(x),

(3.20)

for all
x,y\in K
. We adopt Sweedler’s notation
\beta(x)=\sum_{[x]}x^{[-1]}\otimes x^{[0]}
,
\beta_{2}(x)=\sum_{[x]}x^{[-2]}\otimes x^{[-1]}\otimes x^{[0]}
, etc.
8
8

8

We use square brackets to denote the comodule structure to distinguish it from the comultiplication of the weak Hopf algebra.
The right
H
-comodule algebra can be defined similarly.

Remark 3.1
.

In literature, there are several equivalent expressions of Eq. (
3.20
) (written more explicitly and omitting the sum symbol
1_{K}^{[-1]}\otimes x1_{K}^{[0]}=\varepsilon_{R}(x^{[-1]})\otimes x^{[0]}
):

1.

\beta(1_{K})\in H_{R}\otimes K
;

2.

\beta(1_{K})=(\varepsilon_{R}\otimes\operatorname{id})\circ\beta(1_{K})
;

3.

1_{H}^{(1)}\otimes 1_{H}^{(2)}1_{K}^{[-1]}\otimes 1_{K}^{[0]}=1_{H}^{(1)}\otimes 1_{K}^{[-1]}1_{H}^{(2)}\otimes 1_{K}^{[0]}=1_{K}^{[-2]}\otimes 1_{K}^{[-1]}\otimes 1_{K}^{[0]}
, where we have omitted the sum symbol;

For the convenience of the reader, we provide the proof here.

The equivalence of 1 and 2 is obvious since
\varepsilon_{R}^{2}=\varepsilon_{R}
. For “
1\Rightarrow 3
”, note that
1^{(1)}\otimes 1^{(2)}\in H_{R}\otimes H_{L}
and
hg=gh
for all
h\in H_{L}
and
g\in H_{R}
. Using the fact that for all
h\in H_{R}
we have

\sum_{(1)}1^{(1)}\otimes h1^{(2)}=\Delta(h),

(3.21)

we arrive at the required conclusion.

For “
3\Rightarrow
Eq. (
3.20
)”, note that for
x\in K
, we have

\beta(x1)=x^{[-1]}1^{[-1]}\otimes x^{[0]}1^{[0]}=x^{[-1]}\otimes x^{[0]}.

(3.22)

Then

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{R}(x^{[-1]})\otimes x^{[0]}

\displaystyle=1_{H}^{(1)}\varepsilon(x^{[-1]}1_{H}^{(2)})\otimes x^{[0]}

\displaystyle=1_{H}^{(1)}\varepsilon(x^{[-1]}1_{K}^{[-1]}1_{H}^{(2)})\otimes x^{[0]}1_{K}^{[0]}

\displaystyle=1_{K}^{[-2]}\varepsilon(x^{[-1]}1_{K}^{[-1]})\otimes x^{[0]}1_{K}^{[0]}

\displaystyle=1_{K}^{[-1]}\otimes x1_{K}^{[0]}.

(3.23)

Finally, “Eq. (
3.20
)
\Rightarrow
1” is obvious.

Note that
H
is a comodule algebra over itself with the comodule map given by the comultiplication. Since
\Delta
is an algebra map and

\Delta(1_{H})\in H_{R}\otimes H_{L},

(3.24)

the comodule algebra conditions are satisfied.
The topological boundary condition can also be characterized via the module algebra.
An algebra
A
is called a
left

H
-module algebra if
A
is a left
H
-module such that
h\triangleright(xy)=\sum_{(h)}(h^{(1)}\triangleright x)(h^{(2)}\triangleright y)
and
h\triangleright 1_{A}=\varepsilon_{L}(h)\triangleright 1_{A}
for all
h\in H
and
x\in A
. The
right

H
-module algebra can be defined similarly.

3.2
Fusion category symmetry as dual weak Hopf symmetry

Let us now consider how to understand (multi)fusion category symmetry in the framework of weak Hopf symmetries.
By definition, a fusion category symmetry is a fusion category
\mathcal{C}
that acts on a quantum system
\mathcal{T}
, like lattice system or quantum field theory, as a symmetry.
Treating the symmetry action as an algebra, the symmetry algebra for fusion category
\mathcal{C}
is the Grothendieck ring

\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
. By definition,
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
is generated by the equivalence classes of simple objects in
\mathcal{C}
as a free
\mathbb{Z}
-module. The multiplication is defined by the fusion rule:

[a]\cdot[b]:=[a\otimes b]=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal{C})}N_{ab}^{c}[c],\quad N_{ab}^{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

(3.25)

This is also called the fusion ring, and it is a
\mathbb{Z}_{+}
-ring
[
104
]
. When
\mathcal{C}
is a multifusion category, the unit of the ring is a nonnegative linear combination of the simple objects that constitute the tensor unit
\mathbb{1}
of
\mathcal{C}
. When
\mathcal{C}
is a fusion category,
[\mathbb{1}]
is one of the basis elements. Hereinafter, we will primarily focus on the fusion category case, as the generalization to multifusion categories is straightforward.

The simple topological symmetry defect lines or symmetry operators
W_{[a]}
’s are labeled by basis elements
[a]\in\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
, which is isomorphism class of simple objects in
\mathcal{C}
.
These symmetry defect line obey the fusion algebra:

W_{[a]}W_{[b]}=W_{[a\otimes b]}=W_{\sum_{c}N_{ab}^{c}[c]},N_{ab}^{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

(3.26)

To make the fusion algebra a
\mathbb{C}
-algebra, we introduce the character algebra
R(\mathcal{C}):=\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}

[
128
]
. The fusion category symmetry is thus equivalently described by the character algebra
R(\mathcal{C})
, with the symmetry operator
W_{\alpha}
defined for
\alpha\in R(\mathcal{C})
.

Recall that a weak Hopf algebra
H
is called connected if and only if the trivial representation
\mathbb{1}
of
H
is a simple object. In this case, the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
is a unitary fusion category. On the other hand, for any fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, there exists a (not unique) weak Hopf algebra
H
such that
\mathsf{Rep}(H)\simeq\mathcal{C}
as tensor categories
[
92
,
91
,
90
,
127
]
.
Two weak Hopf algebras
H
and
H^{\prime}
are called Morita equivalent if and only if
\mathsf{Rep}(H)\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(H^{\prime})
as tensor categories. Thus for a given fusion category symmetry, we can determine the weak Hopf symmetry
H
up to Morita equivalence.

The construction of a weak Hopf algebra
H
from a given fusion category
\mathcal{C}
, such that
\mathsf{Rep}(H)\simeq\mathcal{C}
, will be presented in Section
3.3
. Now suppose we already have a weak Hopf algebra
H
at hand, and consider how to interpret the fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}
(or more precisely, the fusion ring
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
) as a dual weak Hopf symmetry. Before proceeding, let us first recall some basic facts about the representation theory of weak Hopf algebras.

The
H_{L}
is the tensor unit with
H
-action given by

x\triangleright a=\varepsilon_{L}(xh)=x^{(1)}aS(x^{(2)}),\forall x\in H,\forall a\in H_{L}.

(3.27)

For two representations
V,W
, the action of
H
on
V\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}W
is defined as

h\triangleright(v\otimes w):=\sum_{(h)}h^{(1)}v\otimes h^{(2)}w,

(3.28)

the tensor product of
V
and
W
is defined as

V\otimes_{H_{L}}W=\{x\in V\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}W|\Delta(1)\triangleright x=x\}.

(3.29)

Note that
\Delta(1)
does not act as the identity on
V\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}W
. However, since
\Delta(1)^{2}=\Delta(1)
, it serves as the identity on the balanced tensor product
V\otimes_{H_{L}}W
.
The dual representation of
V
is
\hat{V}:=\operatorname{Hom}(V,\mathbb{C})
equipped with the action
(h\triangleright f)(x):=f(S(h)\triangleright x)
.

Recall that, an element
l
(or
r
) is called a left (or right) integral of
H
if it satisfies
xl=\varepsilon_{L}(x)l
(or
rx=r\varepsilon_{R}(x)
). A left (or right) integral
l
(or
r
) is considered left (or right) normalized if
\varepsilon_{L}(l)=1_{H}
(or
\varepsilon_{R}(r)=1_{H}
). When an element
h
functions as both a left and right integral, it is referred to as a two-sided integral. A Haar integral in
H
is a two-sided integral that is normalized on both sides. For a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra
H
, there always exist a unique Haar integral.

Lemma 1

(Schur’s lemma for weak Hopf algebra)
.

Let
\Gamma:H\to\operatorname{End}(V)
and
\Phi:H\to\operatorname{End}(W)
be two irreducible representations of a weak Hopf algebra
H
, and let
f:V\to W
be a linear map such that
\Phi(x)\circ f=f\circ\Gamma(x)
for all
x\in H
. If
\Gamma
and
\Phi
are not isomorphic, then
f=0
. When
\Gamma=\Phi
,
f
is a scalar multiple of the identity map on
V
, i.e.,
f\propto\operatorname{id}_{V}
.

Proof.

The proof follows the same reasoning as in Ref.
[
56
]
.
∎

For Haar integral
\lambda\in H
and arbitrary
x\in H
, we have the following
[
127
,
128
]

\sum_{(\lambda)}xS(\lambda^{(1)})\otimes\lambda^{(2)}=\sum_{(\lambda)}S(\lambda^{(1)})\otimes\lambda^{(2)}x.

(3.30)

Then for a linear map
f:V\to W
, we define

F=\sum_{(\lambda)}\Phi(S(\lambda^{(1)}))\circ f\circ\Gamma(\lambda^{(2)}).

(3.31)

It’s clear from Eq. (
3.30
) that

\Phi(x)\circ F=F\circ\Gamma(x),\quad\forall x\in H.

(3.32)

Lemma 2
.

(1) For any
f:V\to W
, and define
F
as in Eq. (
3.31
), we have: (i) If
\Gamma
and
\Phi
are not isomorphic,
F=0
; (ii) when
\Gamma=\Phi
, we have

F=\frac{1}{d_{\Gamma}}\operatorname{Tr}(f)\operatorname{id}_{V}.

(3.33)

(2) From the above result, we obtain the orthogonality relation for irreps of
H
:

\sum_{(\lambda)}\Phi_{ij}(S(\lambda^{(1)}))\Gamma_{kl}(\lambda^{(2)})=\frac{\delta_{\Phi,\Gamma}\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}}{d_{\Gamma}}=\sum_{(\lambda)}\Phi_{ij}(S(\lambda^{(2)}))\Gamma_{kl}(\lambda^{(1)}).

(3.34)

where we have used the cocommutativity of
\lambda
.

Proof.

(1) Note that (i) is a direct result of Proposition
1
. For (ii), we have

\operatorname{Tr}F=\sum_{(\lambda)}\operatorname{Tr}[\Gamma(S(\lambda^{(1)}))\circ f\circ\Gamma(\lambda^{(2)})]=\operatorname{Tr}[\Gamma(\varepsilon_{L}(\lambda))f]=\operatorname{Tr}f,

(3.35)

which implies Eq. (
3.33
), notice that we have used
\varepsilon_{L}(\lambda)=1_{H}
.

(2) From (1), the matrix elements
F_{il}
is of the form

\displaystyle\sum_{(\lambda)}\sum_{jk}\Phi_{ij}(S(\lambda^{(1)}))f_{jk}\Gamma_{kl}(\lambda^{(2)})=\frac{\delta_{\Phi,\Gamma}}{d_{\Gamma}}\delta_{il}\sum_{jk}f_{jk}\delta_{jk}.

(3.36)

This implies the required result by taking
f_{jk}=\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\delta_{kk^{\prime}}
.
∎

Suppose we have identified a weak Hopf algebra
H
that realizes the fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(H)
. In this case, the simple topological defect lines are labeled by the irreducible representations
\Gamma\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)
of the weak Hopf algebra
H
.
The fusion ring of
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
can equivalently be described using the irreducible characters
\chi_{\Gamma}
, where
\Gamma\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)
:

\chi_{\Gamma}\cdot\chi_{\Phi}=\chi_{\Gamma\otimes\Phi}=\sum_{\Psi\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)}N_{\Gamma\Phi}^{\Psi}\chi_{\Psi}.

(3.37)

Here, the product on the left-hand side is defined by
\chi_{\Gamma}\cdot\chi_{\Phi}(x)=\sum_{(x)}\chi_{\Gamma}(x^{(1)})\chi_{\Phi}(x^{(2)})
, which corresponds to the multiplication in the dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
.
Recall that for a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra
H
, its dual space
\hat{H}:=\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb{C})
acquires a canonical
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra structure induced by the canonical pairing
\langle\bullet,\bullet\rangle:\hat{H}\times H\to\mathbb{C}
, defined by
\langle\varphi,h\rangle:=\varphi(h)

9
9

9

In this work, we will interchangeably use
\hat{H}
and
H^{\vee}
to denote the dual space of
H
.
For larger mathematical expressions, we will use the notation
(\bullet)^{\vee}
to indicate the dual space.
. The structure morphisms are given by:

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\mu}(\varphi\otimes\psi),x\rangle=\langle\varphi\otimes\psi,\Delta(x)\rangle,

(3.38)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\eta}(1),x\rangle=\varepsilon(x),\;\text{i.e.,}\;\hat{1}=\varepsilon,

(3.39)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{\Delta}(\varphi),x\otimes y\rangle=\langle\varphi,\mu(x\otimes y)\rangle,

(3.40)

\displaystyle\hat{\varepsilon}(\varphi)=\langle\varphi,\eta(1)\rangle,

(3.41)

\displaystyle\langle\hat{S}(\varphi),x\rangle=\langle\varphi,S(x)\rangle.

(3.42)

The star operation on
\hat{H}
is defined as

\langle\varphi^{*},x\rangle=\overline{\langle\varphi,S(x)^{*}\rangle}.

(3.43)

It is clear that every character
\chi_{\Gamma}
of
H
is a complex-valued function on
H
, hence
\chi_{\Gamma}\in\hat{H}
.
Since the irreducible characters form a basis of
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Rep}(H))
, we obtain an embedding

\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Rep}(H))\hookrightarrow\hat{H}
.
By extending scalars, we may consider

R(\mathsf{Rep}(H))=\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Rep}(H))\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}
, which becomes a subalgebra of
\hat{H}
.
Consequently, any fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}
can be realized as a subalgebra of the dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
.

Theorem 1
.

For (1+1)D phase, the fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}
(more precisely,
\operatorname{Gr}(\mathcal{C})
) can be equivalently characterized by some dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
, where
H
is the weak Hopf algebra that satisfies
\mathsf{Rep}(H)\simeq\mathcal{C}
as fusion categories.

The above discussion suggests that weak Hopf symmetry is the most general symmetry for
(1+1)
-dimensional systems, with fusion category symmetry as a special case. As seen in the previous subsection, both group symmetry and Hopf symmetry are special cases of weak Hopf symmetry. Furthermore, invertible group symmetry can be viewed as a fusion category symmetry by categorifying the group. For a finite group
G
, we introduce the discrete category
\underline{G}
, whose objects are the group elements, and define the fusion as

g\otimes h:=gh.

(3.44)

The fusion category symmetry
\underline{G}
corresponds exactly to group symmetry. Notice that
\underline{G}
has the same fusion rule as
\mathsf{Vect}_{G}
. Recall that
\mathsf{Vect}_{G}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}({\mathbb{C}[G]}^{\vee})
, where
H
is chosen as
\mathbb{C}[G]
. Thus, the fusion category symmetry
\underline{G}
is equivalent to dual weak Hopf symmetry
\hat{H}=\mathbb{C}[G]^{\vee\vee}\cong\mathbb{C}[G]
, which aligns perfectly with the structure of invertible symmetry.

Moreover, when considering general (not necessarily connected) weak Hopf symmetries, this framework also includes multifusion category symmetries as a special case.

We denote all cocommutative elements of
\hat{H}
as
\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})
, namely:

\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})=\{f:H\to\mathbb{C}|f(xy)=f(yx)\}.

(3.45)

This means that all functions in
\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})
are class functions of
W
.

Proposition 1
.

Let
H
be a semisimple weak Hopf algebra.
Then the space of cocommutative elements in the dual,
\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})
, is spanned by the irreducible characters
\chi_{\Gamma}
of
H
, that is,

\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})\cong R(\mathsf{Rep}(H)):=\operatorname{Gr}(\mathsf{Rep}(H))\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}.

Proof.

We prove the statement in two steps.

1. First, we show that
\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})\cong(H/[H,H])^{\vee}
.
Let
[H,H]:=\operatorname{Span}\{xy-yx\mid x,y\in H\}
and consider the canonical projection
\pi:H\to H/[H,H]
.
By definition, we have

\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})=\{f:H\to\mathbb{C}\mid f([H,H])=0\}.

Now, define the map

\Psi:(H/[H,H])^{\vee}\to\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H}),\quad\Psi(f)=f\circ\pi.

This map is clearly well-defined, linear, and bijective, hence an isomorphism.

2. Next, we use the fact that the irreducible characters of
H
form a basis of
(H/[H,H])^{\vee}
for any finite-dimensional semisimple algebra.
See, e.g., Ref.
[
132
, Theorem 3.6.2]
for a proof of this fact.
∎

The above result implies that, if we are only concerned with the symmetry encoded by the fusion algebra structure, the fusion category symmetry
\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{Rep}(H)
can be identified with the character algebra
\operatorname{Cocom}(\hat{H})
.

3.3
Reconstructing weak Hopf symmetry from given fusion category

The weak Hopf algebra associated with a given fusion category can be reconstructed in the following two ways:

1.
Tannaka-Krein reconstruction from weak fiber functor.
— Given any fusion category
\mathcal{C}
over
\mathbb{C}
, there exists an algebra
A
over
\mathbb{C}
such that we can endow
\mathcal{C}
with an exact faithful monoidal functor
F:\mathcal{C}\to{{}_{A}}\mathsf{Mod}_{A}
(we call it the weak fiber functor over fusion category
10
10

10

Notice that in Ref.
[
55
]
, we refer to this functor as a fiber functor. We emphasize that this is not the same as a fiber functor
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathsf{Vect}
, which does not always exist for general fusion categories.
). The algebra
H=\operatorname{End}(F)
, consisting of natural transformations from
F
to itself. It can be proved that
H
forms a weak Hopf symmetry, and the representation category
\mathsf{Rep}(H)
is equivalent to
\mathcal{C}
as unitary fusion categories
[
90
,
91
]
.

2.
Boundary tube algebra.
— An intuitive approach involves the concept of boundary tube algebra
[
121
,
133
,
55
,
134
]

\mathcal{C}
, we consider a gapped boundary described by a
\mathcal{C}
-module category
{{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{M}
and construct the corresponding boundary tube algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{M})
, which is a
C^{*}
weak Hopf algebra. Setting
\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{C}
, namely, considering the smooth boundary, we have the boundary tube algebra spanned by the following basis:

(3.46)

Notice that for a multiplicity-free fusion category, the vertex label can be omitted, since there is only one possible choice.
The fusion category
\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{Fun}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})
(that is, the functor category of module endofunctors of
{}_{\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{C}
, which mathematically characterizes the boundary phase) can be embedded into the representation category of the tube algebra
\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}))
. In particular, there exists a monoidal functor

F:\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C})).

(3.47)

See Ref.
[
134
]
for a detailed proof.
Therefore, the fusion category
\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{M}}^{*}
can be realized in terms of the weak Hopf algebra
\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C})
. Moreover, it is widely expected that
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(\mathbf{Tube}({{}_{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}))
, with a proof based on the internal-hom construction of the boundary tube algebra given in Ref.
[
135
]
. However, a transparent proof relying solely on diagrammatic calculations is still absent.

Since the boundary tube algebra plays a crucial role in constructing explicit examples of the cluster state model in Section
8
, we briefly recall its structure here for convenience. For further details, see Refs.
[
55
,
134
]
.

(3.54)

where
\mathrm{rank}\mathcal{C}
denotes the number of objects in
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{C}
.

3.4
Weak Hopf symmetric single qudit system

Now let us consider a simplest example of weak Hopf symmetric system, a
C^{*}
weak Hopf qudit.
By a weak Hopf qudit we mean a complex weak Hopf algebra
H
with inner product given by

\langle a,b\rangle=\Lambda(a^{*}b),

(3.55)

where
\Lambda
is the Haar integral of
\hat{H}
(also called Haar measure of
H
).
We will hereinafter denote Haar integral of
H
as
\lambda
and Haar integral of
\hat{H}
as
\Lambda
.
For the specail case of group algebra
H=\mathbb{C}[G]
, the Haar integral is of the form

\lambda=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g,\quad\Lambda=\delta_{1_{G}}(\bullet).

(3.56)

The inner product for this case it the usual
11
11

11

Recall that the involution of
\mathbb{C}[G]
is defined by
g^{*}=g^{-1}
for all
g\in G
, extended antilinearly over the entire space.

\langle g,h\rangle=\delta_{1_{G}}(g^{*}h)=\delta_{1_{G},g^{-1}h}=\delta_{g,h}
for all
g,h\in G
.

Weak Hopf qudit

\mathcal{H}=H

Regular action

\begin{aligned} &\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|gh\rangle,\ \overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|hS^{-1}(g)\rangle,\\
&\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{X}}_{g}|h\rangle=|S^{-1}(g)h\rangle,\ \tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{X}}_{g}|h\rangle=|hg\rangle\end{aligned}

Dual action

\begin{aligned} &\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|\psi\rightharpoonup h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(h^{(2)})|h^{(1)}\rangle\\
&\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|h\leftharpoonup\hat{S}(\psi)\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(S(h^{(1)}))|h^{(2)}\rangle\\
&\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|\hat{S}(\psi)\rightharpoonup h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(S(h^{(2)}))|h^{(1)}\rangle,\\
&\tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|h\leftharpoonup\psi\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(h^{(1)})|h^{(2)}\rangle\end{aligned}

Table 2
:
Summary of quantum operations for weak Hopf qudit system.

The regular action of a weak Hopf algebra on itself can be viewed as a generalization of Pauli
X
-type operators. For the left action
H\curvearrowright H
, we define:

\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|gh\rangle,\quad\overset{\leftarrow}{X}_{g}|h\rangle=|hS^{-1}(g)\rangle.

(3.57)

For the right action
H\curvearrowleft H
, we define:

\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{X}}_{g}|h\rangle=|S^{-1}(g)h\rangle,\quad\tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{X}}_{g}|h\rangle=|hg\rangle.

(3.58)

The use of
S^{-1}
in the above definitions ensures the commutative local stabilizer in weak Hopf lattice gauge theory
[
54
]

12
12

12

Alternatively, we can choose to include
S^{-1}
in the weak Hopf Pauli
Z
operators, in which case there is no need to use
S^{-1}
in the definition of the weak Hopf Pauli
X
operators.

. Additionally, note that for a
C^{*}
Hopf algebra and more general weak Kac algebra,
S^{-1}=S
.

There are also canonical actions of the dual weak Hopf algebra
\hat{H}
on the Hopf qudit
H
, defined using Sweedler’s notation as follows:

\varphi\rightharpoonup x:=\sum_{(x)}x^{(1)}\langle\varphi,x^{(2)}\rangle,\quad x\leftharpoonup\varphi:=\sum_{(x)}\langle\varphi,x^{(1)}\rangle x^{(2)},

(3.59)

for all
\varphi\in\hat{H}
and
x\in H
.
The operators corresponding the
\hat{H}
action on weak Hopf qudit
H
can be regarded as generalized Pauli
Z
-type operators.
For left action
\hat{H}\curvearrowright H
, we define:

\displaystyle\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|\psi\rightharpoonup h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(h^{(2)})|h^{(1)}\rangle,

(3.60)

\displaystyle\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|h\leftharpoonup\hat{S}(\psi)\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(S(h^{(1)}))|h^{(2)}\rangle.

(3.61)

For right action
H\curvearrowleft\hat{H}
, we define

\displaystyle\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|\hat{S}(\psi)\rightharpoonup h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(S(h^{(2)}))|h^{(1)}\rangle,

(3.62)

\displaystyle\tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}}_{\psi}|h\rangle=|h\leftharpoonup\psi\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\psi(h^{(1)})|h^{(2)}\rangle.

(3.63)

Since the character
\chi_{\Gamma}
of irreducible representations
\Gamma\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)
lies in
\hat{H}
, we can define
\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma},\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma},\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}}_{\Gamma},\tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}}_{\Gamma}
by replacing
\psi
with
\chi_{\Gamma}
in the expressions given above (In certain cases, to avoid ambiguity, we will also use notations such as
\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\chi_{\Gamma}}
, and similar variants, for clarity).

It is convenient to introduce representation-matrix-valued
Z
-type operators:

Z_{\Gamma}|h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\Gamma(h^{(2)})|h^{(1)}\rangle,\quad Z_{\Gamma}^{\ddagger}|h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\Gamma(S(h^{(1)}))|h^{(2)}\rangle.

(3.64)

Similarly, we define

\tilde{Z}_{\Gamma}|h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\Gamma(h^{(1)})|h^{(2)}\rangle,\quad\tilde{Z}_{\Gamma}^{\ddagger}|h\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\Gamma(S(h^{(2)}))|h^{(1)}\rangle.

(3.65)

Using
\operatorname{Tr}^{\prime}
to denote the trace over the representation space, we obtain

\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma}=\operatorname{Tr}^{\prime}Z_{\Gamma},\quad\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}_{\Gamma}=\operatorname{Tr}^{\prime}Z^{\ddagger}_{\Gamma},\quad\tilde{\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}}_{\Gamma}=\operatorname{Tr}^{\prime}\tilde{Z}_{\Gamma},\quad\tilde{\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}}_{\Gamma}=\operatorname{Tr}^{\prime}\tilde{Z}^{\ddagger}_{\Gamma}.

(3.66)

Following the notation of Kitaev
[
95
,
50
,
53
,
54
]
, we have
L_{+}=\overset{\rightarrow}{X}
,
L_{-}=\overset{\leftarrow}{X}
,
T_{+}=\overset{\rightarrow}{Z}
, and
T_{-}=\overset{\leftarrow}{Z}
. The notations here primarily follows Refs.
[
96
,
80
,
56
]
, with slight modifications to accommodate the weak Hopf algebra case.

The simplest example of a Hamiltonian with weak Hopf symmetry can be constructed from the center of
H
. Let
\gamma\in\operatorname{Center}(H)
(the center of
H
is defined as
\operatorname{Center}(H)=\{h\in H|hg=gh,\,\forall g\in H\}
), and define
\mathbb{H}=\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{\gamma}
. Then,
[\overset{\rightarrow}{X}_{h},\mathbb{H}]=0
for all
h\in H
. Similarly, a model exhibiting comodule algebra symmetry can be constructed.

4
Weak Hopf algebra tensor network states

The key feature of Hopf and weak Hopf qudits lies in their comultiplication, which can be used to generate entanglement and quantum correlations. In Ref.
[
56
]
, the Hopf tensor network was employed as a fundamental tool to solve the Hopf cluster state model. For the more general weak Hopf cluster ladder model, one needs to apply a suitable generalization of the Hopf tensor network
[
56
,
54
,
53
,
106
,
50
]
.

4.1
Weak Hopf pairing

The main tool we shall use is the pairing between a weak Hopf algebra
H
and its dual
\hat{H}
(Eqs. (
3.38
)–(
3.42
)). This construction can be further extended to any pair of weak Hopf algebras, as follows:

Definition 5

(canonical pairing)
.

A canonical pairing (also called (weak) Hopf pairing) is a function
\langle\bullet,\bullet\rangle:M\otimes N\to\mathbb{C}
between two weak Hopf algebras
M,N
is a bilinear map satisfying

\displaystyle\langle hg,a\rangle=\sum_{(a)}\langle h,a^{(1)}\rangle\langle g,a^{(2)}\rangle,

(4.1)

\displaystyle\langle h,ab\rangle=\sum_{(h)}\langle h^{(1)},a\rangle\langle h^{(2)},b\rangle,

(4.2)

\displaystyle\langle 1_{M},a\rangle=\varepsilon_{N}(a),

(4.3)

\displaystyle\langle h,1_{N}\rangle=\varepsilon_{M}(h),

(4.4)

\displaystyle\langle S_{M}(h),a\rangle=\langle h,S_{N}(a)\rangle.

(4.5)

The pairing between
\hat{H}
and
H
is a particular instance of the canonical pairing defined above. Based on this, we introduce a generalized weak Hopf tensor network formulated via pairings, endowed with advantageous properties that make it suitable for solving the lattice model discussed below.
While our primary emphasis is on the pairing between
\hat{H}
and
H
, the extension to other pairings is straightforward.

We will draw elements
h\in H
and
\psi\in\hat{H}
and their pairing
\langle\psi,h\rangle=\psi(h)\in\mathbb{C}
as

(4.13)

Notice that, from Eq. (
3.42
), we can derive
\langle\hat{S}^{-1}(\varphi),x\rangle=\langle\varphi,S^{-1}(x)\rangle
.

Using the pairing, one can construct a general weak Hopf tensor network by first applying comultiplication to elements, then multiplying certain components, and finally implementing the pairing.

The tensor network representation presented here is more compact and closely resembles a string diagram compared to that in Ref.
[
56
]
, since we do not express every structure explicitly in terms of tensors. While this is convenient for calculations, the entanglement pattern cannot be read out directly as in the usual tensor network formalism. To obtain a representation that encodes entanglement features, one needs to employ a basis expansion and express all structures in terms of that basis. A detailed discussion of this point will be provided shortly. This representation can be effectively employed to solve the cluster ladder model (see Sections
6
and
7
for details).
It is also worth noting that our tensor network representation differs from that in Ref.
[
136
]
, where a matrix-product operator representation of the weak Hopf algebra is introduced.

4.2
Weak Hopf tensor network states and operators

We now provide further details on weak Hopf tensor networks and their one-dimensional counterparts, namely weak Hopf matrix-product states and matrix-product operators constructed from weak Hopf structures.

Consider weak Hopf algebra
H
with basis
\{v_{i}\}
(for dual weak Hopf algebra, we will fix the dual basis
\{\widehat{v}_{j}
} with
\widehat{v}_{j}(v_{i})=\delta_{ij}
). We can represent a element
x=\sum_{i}x_{i}v_{i}\in H
as a tensor:

This means that we assume the legs represent the degrees of freedom in the basis

.
In the given basis, we can represent comultiplication as a structure matrix

.

\Delta_{n-1}(v_{i})=\sum_{j,k,\cdots,l}C_{i}^{jk\cdots l}v_{j}\otimes v_{k}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{l},

(4.18)

The legs represent components
x^{(1)},\cdots,x^{(n)}
in the comultiplication, thus the order of these legs are crucial.

The comultiplication generates entanglement. For instance, consider the group algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]
and the element

|x\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_{g\in G}|g\rangle
, which can be regarded as a state. After applying the comultiplication, we obtain a generalized Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) state:

\Delta_{n-1}(|x\rangle)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_{g\in G}|g\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|g\rangle,

(4.19)

which is known to be a highly entangled state. The comultiplication for a group-valued qudit acts as a quantum cloning operation on the basis consisting of group elements.

We can also introduce the multiplication structure matrix

v_{i}\cdot v_{j}=\sum_{k}A_{ij}^{k}v_{k},

(4.20)

with which we have
x\cdot y=\sum_{i,j,k}x_{i}y_{j}A_{ij}^{k}v_{k}
.
The associativity of multiplication allows us to introduce
A_{ij\cdots k}^{l}
by
v_{i}v_{j}\cdots v_{k}=\sum_{l}A_{ij\cdots k}^{l}v_{l}
without ambiguity, we draw it as

(4.23)

The axioms of a weak Hopf algebra can be reformulated in terms of these structure tensors as follows (where we adopt the Einstein summation convention):

•

Algebra:

1x=x1=x
as
\iota_{i}A_{ij}^{k}x_{j}=x_{i}A_{ij}^{k}\iota_{j}=x_{k}
; associativity as
A_{ij}^{k}A_{kl}^{p}=A_{jl}^{m}A_{im}^{p}
.

•

Coalgebra:

\varepsilon(x^{\langle 1\rangle})x^{\langle 2\rangle}=x=x^{\langle 1\rangle}\varepsilon(x^{\langle 2\rangle})
as
x_{i}C_{i}^{jk}\epsilon_{j}=x_{k}=x_{i}C_{i}^{kj}\epsilon_{j}
; coassociativity as
C_{i}^{jk}C_{j}^{st}=C_{i}^{jk}C_{k}^{st}
.

•

Compatibility of multiplication and comultiplication:

C_{k}^{mn}A_{ij}^{k}=C_{i}^{ab}C_{j}^{cd}A_{ac}^{m}A_{bd}^{n}.

•

Weak counit:

\epsilon_{z}A_{ijk}^{z}=C_{j}^{ab}\;(\epsilon_{s}A_{ia}^{s})\;(\epsilon_{t}A_{bk}^{t})=C_{j}^{ab}\;(\epsilon_{s}A_{ib}^{s})\;(\epsilon_{t}A_{ak}^{t}).

•

Weak identity:

\iota_{p}C_{p}^{mnq}=(\iota_{i}C_{i}^{mb})\,(\iota_{j}C_{j}^{cq})\,A_{bc}^{n}=(\iota_{k}C_{k}^{sq})\,(\iota_{l}C_{l}^{mp})\,A_{sp}^{n}.

•

Antipode axioms:

x_{i}C_{i}^{ab}S_{a}^{r}A_{rb}^{k}=\epsilon_{s}x_{i}A_{ia}^{s}(\iota_{p}C_{p}^{ka})
,

x_{i}C_{i}^{ab}A_{ar}^{k}S_{b}^{r}=(\iota_{p}C_{p}^{bk})\epsilon_{s}A_{bi}^{s}
,

x_{i}S_{i}^{j}=C_{i}^{abc}S_{a}^{s}S_{c}^{r}A_{sbr}^{j}.

These axioms are particularly useful when performing calculations with weak Hopf tensor networks.

where light cyan legs represents comultiplication
\Delta_{n-1}(g)=\sum_{k_{1}\cdots k_{n}}C_{j}^{k_{1}\cdots k_{n}}g_{j}v_{k_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{k_{n}}
. It is clear that
W_{g}W_{h}=W_{gh}
. In the MPO representation, this multiplication corresponds to the vertical gluing of MPOs for
W_{g}
and
W_{h}
. Note also that
W_{1_{H}}\neq I
, since for a general weak Hopf algebra we have
\Delta(1_{H})\neq 1_{H}\otimes 1_{H}
13
13

13

In many situations, this serves as an indicator of anomaly, since in the anomaly-free case the corresponding symmetry is a Hopf symmetry. Indeed, for a fusion category
\mathcal{C}
admitting a fiber functor
F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathsf{Vect}
, there always exists a Hopf algebra
H
such that
\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}(H)
, in which case
W_{1_{H}}=I
. A weak Hopf symmetry is a Hopf symmetry if and only if
\Delta(1_{H})=1_{H}\otimes 1_{H}
.

In the group case, the operator
W_{g}
becomes on-site, and the cyan legs disappear.
